opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so Dr. Eureka is a follow-up to our earlier work, Eureka, and the core idea is pretty simple. In robotics, the two most painful manual steps are reward design and domain randomization. Normally you have a PhD student sitting there tuning reward functions by hand, and then tuning the physics parameters of the simulation, like friction, damping, gravity, and so on, so that a policy trained in simulation can actually survive in the real world. That's the sim-to-real gap, and it's been a huge bottleneck.

What we did with Eureka was show that a large language model can write the reward functions itself. It looks at the environment code, proposes a reward, we train a policy in simulation, feed the training stats back to the model, and it iterates. That's how we got a five-finger robot hand to do pen spinning, which is really hard even for humans to hand-engineer.

Dr. Eureka takes the next step. Now the LLM also writes the domain randomization configuration. It reasons about what physical parameters matter for the task and what ranges are plausible in the real world. One example I like is the robot dog balancing and walking on a yoga ball. That's very hard to model physically because the ball is bouncy and deformable. But by having the LLM automate both the reward and the randomization, we trained it fully in simulation and then transferred it zero-shot to the real world, with no fine-tuning on real data.

Why does this matter for generalization? Because if you randomize over a wide enough range of simulated realities, the real world just becomes one more sample in that distribution. A neural network that can handle ten thousand different simulated physics can very likely handle the eleven-thousandth one, which happens to be our reality.

The bigger picture is that the scarce resource in robotics isn't compute anymore, it's human time and attention. Real-world data collection doesn't scale; you're bound by the number of robots and operators you have and, fundamentally, by 24 hours a day. Simulation scales with compute. So if you can take the human out of the loop for the tedious engineering of rewards and sim parameters, you can run this process massively in parallel, on many tasks at once. That's what I think points toward generalist agents: not one carefully hand-tuned skill, but a pipeline where foundation models orchestrate the training of thousands of skills in simulation, and those skills transfer to physical robots.

Longer term, I think the recipe for a robot foundation model combines a few data sources: internet-scale video and text for common sense and semantics, massive simulation for physics and control, and a smaller amount of real-world teleoperation data to ground everything. Dr. Eureka is one piece of that, showing that the simulation piece can be automated and still produce something that works in the messy real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that randomizing across a wide enough range of simulated realities makes the real world “one more sample in that distribution,” and illustrates this with a policy handling many simulated physics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Dr. Eureka is really a continuation of the Eureka line of work, and the core idea is that we use large language models as the designers of the training process itself rather than as the policy. So in the original Eureka, we had GPT-4 write reward functions for robot skills, like the famous pen-spinning task on a dexterous hand, and it iterated on those rewards in a closed loop with the simulator, basically acting as a reward engineer that never gets tired. Dr. Eureka takes the next step, which is the sim-to-real part. The thing people underestimate is that the hardest part of simulation training isn't usually the reward, it's domain randomization: how much do I randomize friction, mass, motor strength, latency, all these physical parameters so that the policy survives contact with a real robot. That's traditionally this very tedious, expert-driven, trial-and-error thing. Dr. Eureka has the language model write those domain randomization configurations too, and it reasons about the physics the way a grad student would, like "the robot will be walking on a yoga ball, so the surface compliance is uncertain, let me widen that range." And it worked zero-shot. We got a quadruped balancing and walking on a yoga ball in the real world with no real-world fine-tuning, which is a task that would be pretty painful to hand-tune.

So why does that point toward generalist agents? To me, the bottleneck for real-world robotics has never been the learning algorithm per se, it's the data and the human labor around the data. Every task needed a human in the loop writing rewards, tuning randomization, debugging why the simulator didn't match reality. If a language model can automate that whole pipeline, then simulation becomes a data engine where you can scale the number of tasks and skills the same way we scaled text and images. You can imagine a flywheel: the model proposes tasks, proposes rewards, proposes randomizations, trains policies, and the ones that transfer go into a foundation model for robots. That's really the thesis behind what we've been doing at NVIDIA with GEAR and Project GR00T: the path to embodied generalization runs through massive, largely automated simulation, with the LLM as the orchestrator of that process rather than just a component inside the robot. Dr. Eureka is a small but concrete proof that the orchestrator role actually works on real hardware.

r001.rationale: The response says automated simulation could scale tasks and skills and help policies transfer to real hardware, but it does not propose that mastering skills across sufficiently diverse virtual worlds makes the real world part of that broader distribution.

astra-6.text:
I think Dr. Eureka points toward a really interesting loop: an AI system can help design the training process for another AI system. In robotics, specifying the goal is only part of the problem. You also need a reward that encourages the right behavior, and you need a simulation that prepares the policy for what it will encounter in the physical world.

Imagine teaching a robot dog to balance on a ball. In simulation, it might discover a strategy that works beautifully under one particular set of conditions. But the real world has different friction, different motor responses, and imperfect sensing. So the question becomes: what variations should we expose it to during training so that it learns a robust skill?

With Dr. Eureka, the language model helps write the reward and configure that variation in simulation. It brings prior knowledge about the physical world into a process that otherwise takes a lot of manual engineering.

That’s a step toward generalization, but I would distinguish transferring a learned skill to reality from having a generally capable robot. There’s still a substantial gap. What excites me is the possibility of automating more of the learning loop: propose a training setup, train the policy, examine where it fails, and improve the setup. If we can scale that across many tasks and environments, we have a promising path toward agents with a much broader repertoire of real-world skills.

r001.rationale: The response discusses varying simulation conditions and scaling training across tasks and environments, but it does not state that mastering sufficiently diverse virtual worlds would make the real world part of that broader distribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Dr. Eureka points toward a useful recipe: use a language model to help design the process by which a robot learns. That includes the reward—what behavior we want—and the simulation conditions that prepare the policy for the real world.

The challenge is that a simulator is never going to perfectly match reality. Friction changes, motors behave differently, and sensors are noisy. So instead of training for one exact environment, you train across a range of plausible environments. The interesting question is whether an AI system can help choose those variations intelligently, rather than having a human engineer tune everything by hand.

That’s a step toward agents that generalize, but I would distinguish robustness within a task from general intelligence across tasks. A robot handling unfamiliar physical conditions is meaningful progress. The longer-term goal is to bring that robustness together with the ability to learn new skills and reuse them in new situations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training across plausible simulated environments to improve real-world robustness, but does not say that one agent mastering skills across sufficiently diverse virtual worlds makes the real world part of that broader distribution.
